title: Model Deployment & Serving
blurb: Tests the four deployment patterns and when each fits, saving the full pipeline, serving frameworks, why LLM decode is memory-bound, KV cache arithmetic, quantisation, pruning and distillation, and reading a load test.

refLinks.label: §23.2.5 Shrinking the Model: Distillation, Quantisation, Pruning

questions.prompt: Churn scores are computed for a report the sales team reads each morning. Which deployment pattern fits?
options: A real-time endpoint behind a cache
Streaming inference from a Kafka topic
A real-time endpoint that stays up 24/7
Batch inference on a nightly schedule
questions.explanation: Hours-old predictions are fine for a morning report, so batch fits, and compute only runs while the job runs. The chapter calls a real-time endpoint for a batch use case the most common mistake. Streaming is for continuous event scoring, which a daily report doesn't need.

questions.prompt: Which pattern queues a request, processes it when capacity allows, and returns the result by polling or callback?
options: Real-time inference
Batch inference
Async inference
Streaming inference
questions.explanation: That is async inference. It suits long-running jobs such as document processing or LLM generation over long text, and SageMaker's version scales to zero when idle. Batch runs on a schedule over a whole dataset. Streaming handles a continuous event flow. Real-time answers synchronously.

questions.prompt: A low-traffic model gets a few requests an hour, each needing an answer in under 100 ms. What is the main cost problem with a real-time endpoint?
options: The endpoint has to stay running 24/7 even when idle, which is expensive for low traffic.
Real-time endpoints can't scale down below ten instances.
Real-time endpoints charge per prediction at a higher rate than batch.
The endpoint must reload the model on every request, which needs a far larger and costlier instance.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the endpoint stays running around the clock, even during quiet periods, which is expensive for low-traffic models. Nothing in the chapter describes a per-prediction premium or a ten-instance floor, and loading per request is a coding mistake, not a property of the pattern.

questions.prompt: Using recommend_pattern in Listing 23.3, what comes back for max_latency_s=3600, requests_per_day=500,000 and needs_immediate=False?
options: Real-time endpoint (with caching if traffic is spiky)
Real-time endpoint
Async inference
Batch Transform
questions.explanation: The first test needs needs_immediate, which is False. The second test is requests_per_day > 100,000 and not needs_immediate, which is true, so it returns "Batch Transform" before the async branch is reached.

questions.prompt: Using recommend_pattern in Listing 23.3, what comes back for max_latency_s=10, requests_per_day=2,000 and needs_immediate=True?
options: Async inference
Real-time endpoint (with caching if traffic is spiky)
Real-time endpoint
Batch Transform
questions.explanation: The first branch needs max_latency_s < 5, and 10 fails it. The second and third branches both need not needs_immediate, which is False here. So the function falls through to the last return.

questions.prompt: An IoT fleet sends sensor readings continuously, and anomalies should be flagged within a second or two. Readings arrive in bursts. Which pattern does the chapter point to, and why?
options: Async inference, because it scales to zero between bursts and freshness does not matter.
A real-time endpoint per sensor, so each device gets its own model server.
Streaming from Kafka or Kinesis, scoring events in micro-batches as they arrive.
Batch inference every hour, because it is 10 to 100 times cheaper.
questions.explanation: The chapter names IoT anomaly detection as a typical streaming case. Hourly batch fails the freshness need. Async is for long-running jobs where the caller can wait, which contradicts "within a second or two". An endpoint per sensor is not a pattern the chapter describes and would be very costly.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 23.1 save the full pipeline and not only the estimator?
options: Without the scaler or encoder, serving has to rewrite that logic, a source of skew.
Saving the pipeline makes the file smaller, because joblib compresses it.
The estimator alone can't be loaded by joblib.
The pipeline object records the git commit, which the estimator does not.
questions.explanation: Saving preprocessing and model together means serving runs exactly the same transforms as training. Reimplementing them by hand is a classic source of train/serve skew. joblib can save a bare estimator, and a pipeline is not smaller and does not record a commit hash.

questions.prompt: A Java service needs to run a model trained in Python. Which format does the chapter suggest?
options: pickle, which any language can read
ONNX, which is framework-independent
safetensors, which is for tabular pipelines
joblib, which is the default for sklearn
questions.explanation: For cross-language serving (Java, C++, Rust, edge devices) the chapter names ONNX. joblib and pickle are Python-only. safetensors is the modern format for neural network weights, chosen because it is safe to load from untrusted sources.

questions.prompt: A model saved with pickle is loaded under a different Python and library version. What does the chapter warn can happen?
options: It loads correctly, because pickle stores a full copy of the class code.
It always fails with an error, so the mismatch is caught at once.
It may load but predict differently, or fail, since pickle only stores a reference to the class.
It loads correctly but runs slower, because the stored bytecode is recompiled for the new version.
questions.explanation: Pickle and joblib store a reference to the class definition. If the class changed between versions, the object can load and behave differently without any warning. That is why Listing 23.1 also writes the sklearn version into metadata.json.

questions.prompt: Procedure 23.2 loads the pipeline at module scope. What goes wrong if you load it inside predict()?
options: The file is re-read from disk on every request, adding tens of milliseconds to each one.
The model loses its fitted weights between requests.
FastAPI refuses to start, because route functions aren't allowed to open files on disk.
The pydantic validation runs twice per request.
questions.explanation: Loading inside the handler re-reads the file on every call. The chapter names the cost: tens of milliseconds per request and a hammered filesystem. FastAPI allows file reads in handlers, and the fitted weights are in the file either way.

questions.prompt: What does pydantic's PredictRequest class add to the FastAPI endpoint in Listing 23.2?
options: Model loading. It reads the joblib file when the class is defined.
Response caching. Identical requests get the stored answer without running the model again.
Request validation. A body that isn't a list of floats is rejected before predict runs.
Auto-scaling. It starts extra workers under load.
questions.explanation: The chapter lists pydantic request validation among FastAPI's features. The class declares the expected shape, so malformed input is rejected with an error instead of reaching the model. Loading, caching and scaling happen elsewhere, and the chapter notes the team owns scaling with FastAPI.

questions.prompt: Which serving option does the chapter call the recommended default for most AWS production deployments?
options: A hand-written FastAPI app on a single EC2 instance behind a load balancer
SageMaker Endpoints, which run the server, scaling and monitoring for you on AWS
mlflow models serve, which needs no code
BentoML on a self-managed Kubernetes cluster
questions.explanation: SageMaker Endpoints are the managed option and the recommended AWS default. mlflow models serve is good for internal tools. FastAPI is the Python standard, but the team owns server and scaling. BentoML exists so teams don't have to hand-write Kubernetes configs.

questions.prompt: Why is LLM decode memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound?
options: Each new token reprocesses the entire prompt from scratch, which needs more FLOPs than the GPU has.
Decode runs all output tokens in parallel, which saturates memory.
Each new token needs a full read of the weights from GPU memory, with little arithmetic per byte.
The KV cache is stored on the CPU and copied to the GPU each step.
questions.explanation: Decode makes tokens one at a time, and every step reads all the weights. At batch size 1 there is little compute per byte read, so bandwidth sets the speed. The KV cache exists so the prompt is not reprocessed. Processing many tokens in parallel describes prefill, which is compute-bound.

questions.prompt: Why do serving frameworks such as vLLM and TGI focus on batching?
options: Batching makes each single request faster than it would be alone.
Batching shares one weight read across many sequences, so decode does more work per byte read.
Batching lets the model skip the prefill phase for later requests.
Batching shrinks the KV cache, because the sequences in a batch can share a single set of keys and values.
questions.explanation: Each decode step pays a full weight read. Batching amortises it across more tokens at once. The chapter says these frameworks exist largely to batch well, not to speed up any one request. The KV cache grows with batch size, it doesn't shrink.

questions.prompt: A 7B-parameter model is served in fp16 (2 bytes per parameter). How many gigabytes do its weights take? Use 1 GB = 10^9 bytes.
questions.explanation: Weight bytes = bytes_per_param × n_params = 2 × 7 × 10^9 = 14 × 10^9 bytes, which is 14 GB.

questions.prompt: Using the chapter's KV cache formula, how many GB does the cache take for 32 layers, d_model = 4096, sequence length 2048, batch size 8 and fp16 (2 bytes)? Use 1 GB = 10^9 bytes. Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: kv_cache_bytes = 2 × n_layers × d_model × seq_len × batch_size × bytes_per_param = 2 × 32 × 4096 × 2048 × 8 × 2 = 8,589,934,592 bytes, about 8.6 GB. The leading 2 counts the keys and the values.

questions.prompt: The same model and batch size move from a 2,048-token context to 32,768 tokens. The KV cache was about 8.6 GB. About how many GB is it now? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: The cache grows linearly with sequence length. 32,768 / 2,048 = 16, and 8.59 × 16 ≈ 137 GB. That no longer fits on an 80 GB GPU, while the 14 GB of weights hasn't changed.

questions.prompt: An endpoint works fine in testing at batch size 1. Under real concurrent load it runs out of GPU memory. The model file is 14 GB on a 24 GB GPU. What is the likely cause?
options: Prefill is compute-bound, so concurrency makes the GPU set aside extra memory for each request's FLOPs.
The weights are copied once per concurrent request, so 2 requests already need 28 GB.
The KV cache grows with batch size while the weights stay fixed, so concurrency pushed past 24 GB.
The model file grows on disk as requests come in, so it no longer fits.
questions.explanation: Procedure 23.4 warns that sizing off the model file ignores the KV cache. KV memory scales with batch size, so raising concurrency is the common way an endpoint that passed tests runs out of memory. Weights are shared across a batch, not copied per request. Compute-bound prefill does not allocate memory per FLOP.

questions.prompt: Which technique cuts bytes per parameter, for example storing weights as 8-bit integers?
options: Pruning
Batching
Quantisation
Distillation
questions.explanation: Quantisation lowers bytes per parameter. Pruning removes parameters, shrinking N. Distillation trains a smaller student model. Batching shares weight reads across requests and leaves the model unchanged.

refLinks.label: §23.2.5 Shrinking the Model: Distillation, Quantisation, Pruning

questions.prompt: Why does structured pruning often give a real speedup on ordinary hardware when unstructured pruning does not?
options: Unstructured pruning increases the parameter count, because each zeroed weight is stored twice in memory.
Structured pruning removes more parameters, so it is always faster.
Ordinary hardware can't load a model with any zero weights.
Removing heads or layers leaves a smaller dense model. Zeroed weights need sparse kernels to pay off.
questions.explanation: Zeroing individual weights leaves a sparse model of the same shape, and only specialised sparse kernels skip the zeros. Structured pruning makes the model smaller, not sparse, so normal kernels run faster. The chapter adds that structured pruning loses more accuracy per parameter removed.

refLinks.label: §23.2.5 Shrinking the Model: Distillation, Quantisation, Pruning

questions.prompt: Why does a distilled student learn more per example than the same small model trained from scratch on the original labels?
options: It learns from the teacher's soft labels, which carry more signal than one correct answer.
It sees more training examples, because the teacher generates new data.
It can train with a larger learning rate, which the teacher's smooth outputs keep stable.
It copies the teacher's weights directly, then removes the extra layers.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the student learns from the teacher's soft labels, not just the final answer, so each example carries more signal. Distillation trains a separate model. It does not edit or copy the teacher's weights.

refLinks.label: §23.2.5 Shrinking the Model: Distillation, Quantisation, Pruning

questions.prompt: Which statements about the three shrinking techniques match the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: Post-training quantisation needs no retraining and is the cheapest capacity win for a trained model.
Halving bytes per parameter roughly halves decode time at batch size 1.
Quantisation to 4-bit leaves quality unchanged, so 8-bit is never worth choosing.
A distilled student can then be quantised and pruned, and the savings stack.
questions.explanation: The chapter says post-training quantisation is the cheapest win, the techniques stack because N and bytes per parameter are independent multipliers, and halving bytes roughly halves bandwidth-bound decode time. It also says quality loss is usually small at 8-bit and noticeable at 4-bit, so the last statement is wrong.

refLinks.label: §23.2.5 Shrinking the Model: Distillation, Quantisation, Pruning

questions.prompt: The worked example's FastAPI endpoint shows p50 23.1 ms and p99 31.8 ms. What does p99 mean here?
options: Latency was 31.8 ms when concurrency reached 99.
99% of the 200 requests finished within 31.8 ms.
The average latency over the slowest 99 requests was 31.8 ms.
The endpoint answered 99% of requests successfully.
questions.explanation: Listing 23.5 computes np.percentile(latencies, [50, 95, 99]). The 99th percentile is the latency that 99% of requests stayed under. Success rate is a separate figure (100% in the example), and concurrency was fixed at 20.

questions.prompt: The load test ran on one machine with no network hop. A product manager wants to promise sub-100 ms latency to customers based on the 31.8 ms p99. What is the right caveat?
options: The test is meaningless, because logistic regression is too simple to load-test.
The test proves the promise, because the p99 figure already covers the worst case a customer sees.
The test overstates latency, so production will be faster than 31.8 ms.
It measures only the endpoint. Real requests add network time, so check the budget end to end.
questions.explanation: The chapter says production latency over the internet would add network time on top. The result shows the endpoint fits easily inside 100 ms, not that the whole path does. p99 is not the worst case, and network hops make production slower, not faster.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the deployment pattern best suited to: (a) a fraud check that must respond before checkout completes; (b) a nightly report scoring 2 million customer records.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) Real-time endpoint: must respond before checkout completes, a hard synchronous latency requirement. (b) Batch Transform: 2 million records with no need for an immediate individual response is exactly batch's use case.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in one sentence why saving only the fitted estimator (not the full pipeline including the scaler) is a common source of train/serve skew.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If only the estimator is saved, the preprocessing logic (scaling, encoding) that ran before training has to be reimplemented by hand in the serving code. Any small difference between that reimplementation and the original training-time preprocessing produces predictions that differ between the two environments, even though the model itself is identical.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 23.5's measured p50/p95/p99 (23.1/29.6/31.8ms), compute the ratio of p99 to p50, and explain what a ratio this close to 1.0 (versus, say, 5.0) suggests about the endpoint's latency consistency under load.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: $31.8/23.1 \approx 1.38$. A ratio this close to 1.0 indicates very consistent latency under load. The slowest 1% of requests are barely slower than the median, with no long tail of occasional very slow responses. A ratio of 5.0 would indicate a much more volatile endpoint, where some requests are dramatically slower than typical, often a symptom of resource contention, garbage collection pauses, or insufficient worker processes under concurrent load.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 23.4's formula, compute the KV cache size for the same 7B model at batch size 32 (instead of 8) and 2048-token context, and state whether it still fits on an 80GB GPU alongside the 14GB of weights.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: At batch size 32 (4x the original 8): KV cache $= 2 \times 32 \times 4096 \times 2048 \times 32 \times 2 \approx 34.36$GB (4x the batch-8 figure of ~8.6GB). Total $= 14\text{GB weights} + 34.36\text{GB KV cache} \approx 48.4$GB. This still fits on an 80GB GPU, though it now uses well over half the available memory just for the KV cache alone, leaving much less headroom than the batch-8 case's 22.6GB total.

bookExercises.prompt: A team wants a 24/7 real-time endpoint for a model whose predictions are only ever read in a report generated once per day at 6am. Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say to them.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "A daily-report use case with no need for immediate response is exactly what Batch Transform is built for. A 24/7 real-time endpoint would sit idle nearly the entire day, since predictions are only ever consumed once at 6am, and that idle compute is pure waste. Batch Transform for this workload typically costs 10-100x less for the identical output, per this chapter's own Trade-offs guidance."

bookExercises.prompt: A customer reports their LLM endpoint "worked fine in testing but crashes under real traffic." Using Procedure 23.4's common mistake, name the most likely cause and the one number you'd ask them to check first.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is the KV cache not fitting once real concurrent traffic pushes the effective batch size up. Testing typically runs at batch size 1 or low concurrency, which the KV cache formula shows fits easily. Production concurrency can push batch size into a range where the KV cache no longer fits alongside the model weights. The one number to check first: the KV cache size at the *actual* production batch size and context length, computed via Procedure 23.4's formula, not just at whatever batch size was used during testing.

bookExercises.prompt: Read Kipply's "Transformer Inference Arithmetic" section on the "critical batch size." Explain in your own words what happens to decode latency once batch size grows past that point, and how it differs from the memory-bandwidth-bound regime this chapter's formulas describe.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Past the critical batch size, decode latency stops being memory-bandwidth-bound and becomes compute-bound instead. Additional batching no longer amortises the weight-read for free, since the GPU's FLOPs are now the binding constraint rather than memory bandwidth. Further increasing batch size starts trading off against per-token latency directly, instead of being nearly free the way it was below the critical batch size. This differs from the memory-bandwidth-bound regime this chapter's formulas describe, where the whole point of batching is exploiting slack compute capacity while memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. Past the critical batch size, that slack is gone.
